decks.title: Tenses and Clauses in Gap Filling — Part 1
goals: Read the clue words in a sentence and choose the right tense form
Keep the tenses of a paragraph in step with one another
Choose between the present perfect and the simple past on meaning
Use relative, noun and adverb clauses correctly in gaps
Fill gaps in a short paragraph with a five-move routine

slides.heading: Tenses and Clauses in Gap Filling
slides.body_md: CBSE Class 11 English Core, **grammar (7 marks)**. Gap filling with tenses and clauses, and re-ordering and transformation. This part covers the gaps; Part 2 covers re-ordering and transformation.

rows: gap filling with tenses and clauses
re-ordering of jumbled words and transformation of sentences

visual.alt: Table of the grammar part of the Class 11 school paper: gap filling with tenses and clauses, and re-ordering and transformation of sentences, together worth seven marks.
visual.caption: Class 11 has no board exam: this is the school annual examination pattern.

slides.narration: Welcome to grammar. In the school paper, grammar carries seven marks, split between gap filling with tenses and clauses, and re-ordering and transformation of sentences. This first part is about gap filling. The second part is about re-ordering and transformation. Both are skills you can practise until they become routine.

slides.heading: The twelve tense forms
slides.body_md: Every tense is a mix of **time** (present, past, future) and **form** (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).

visual.alt: Table of twelve tense forms of the verb write: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous in the present, past and future.

slides.narration: English has twelve tense forms. Three times, present, past and future, combine with four forms: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous. The simple form states a fact or a finished event. The continuous form shows an action in progress. The perfect form looks back from a point, and the perfect continuous adds how long.

slides.heading: Clue words choose the tense
slides.body_md: The right tense is almost always **signalled** by a word or a second verb in the sentence.

rows: since, for (up to now), so far, yet
present perfect or present perfect continuous
by the time, before, after (an earlier past event)
by tomorrow, by next month, by the time (a future point)

visual.alt: Table of time clues and the tense each points to: every day for present simple, now for present continuous, since and for for present perfect, yesterday for simple past, by the time for past perfect and by tomorrow for future perfect.

slides.narration: Clue words choose the tense. Every day points to the present simple, and now to the present continuous. Since, for and yet point to the present perfect. Yesterday and ago point to the simple past. By the time with an earlier past event points to the past perfect. Underline the clue before you choose.

slides.heading: Check: the clue since

rows: since, for (up to now), so far, yet
present perfect or present perfect continuous
by the time, before, after (an earlier past event)
by tomorrow, by next month, by the time (a future point)

visual.alt: Table of time clues and the tense each points to: every day for present simple, now for present continuous, since and for for present perfect, yesterday for simple past, by the time for past perfect and by tomorrow for future perfect.

slides.narration: Your turn. A boy has played for the college team since two thousand twenty three, and he still plays now. Which form fits the gap?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: two events in the past
slides.body_md: *By the time the ferry ______ (leave) the jetty, Asha ______ (wait) for forty minutes.*
bullets: **Clue:** *by the time* with a past event: a past reference point.
**Gap 1:** the ferry leaving is that point: **left**.
**Gap 2:** the waiting ran up to that point, with a duration: **had been waiting**.
**Check:** *had waited* is also accepted, but *had been waiting* stresses the length.

nodes.label: Name the time and the order of events

visual.alt: Flow of the gap-filling routine: read the whole sentence, underline the clue words, name the time and the order of events, choose the form, then reread the paragraph.
visual.caption: SOYL five-move routine for a gap.

slides.narration: Look at this example. By the time the ferry left the jetty, Asha had been waiting for forty minutes. The words by the time give a past reference point, so the ferry left. The waiting ran up to that point and has a length of forty minutes, so we use the past perfect continuous: had been waiting. Always check the clue first.

slides.heading: Present perfect or simple past?
columns:
**Present perfect**

- the result or experience matters now
- *since*, *for*, *so far*, *just*, *yet*
- *The bus has left* (it is not here)

**Simple past**

- a finished event
- *yesterday*, *ago*, *last year*, *in 2020*
- *The bus left at six*

rows: since, for, so far, just, yet, ever
The bus has left (it is gone)

visual.alt: Table comparing the present perfect and the simple past: the present perfect links to now and uses since, for, just and yet; the simple past is a finished event with words like yesterday and ago.

slides.narration: Two tenses often confuse students. Use the present perfect when the result or experience still matters now, with words such as since, for, so far, just and yet. Use the simple past for a finished event, especially with a time word like yesterday, ago or last year. A definite past time word rules the present perfect out.

slides.heading: Keeping tenses in step
slides.body_md: A paragraph must hold **one time frame** unless the meaning moves. Look at the verbs around the gap, not only the gap.

rows: earlier = past perfect; later = simple past
The film had begun when we arrived
past continuous or past perfect continuous + simple past
We were waiting when the bell rang
present form in the clause, will in the main clause
I will call when I reach home
She said that she was tired

visual.alt: Table of tense sequence patterns: two past events use the past perfect for the earlier one, a long action cut short uses the continuous, a future time clause uses a present form, and a past reporting verb backshifts.

slides.narration: In a paragraph, tenses must agree. When two past events are linked, the earlier one takes the past perfect and the later one the simple past. A long action cut short takes the continuous. A clause of time about the future uses a present form, and a past reporting verb backshifts the reported verb. Read the whole paragraph before you fill any gap.

slides.heading: Conditions: three patterns
slides.body_md: The tense in an *if* clause tells you **how likely** the condition is.

rows: If it rains, we will stay in
If I had a bike, I would ride to school
If I had known, I would have called

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of condition: likely uses present simple and will, unlikely uses simple past and would, and impossible past uses past perfect and would have.

slides.narration: Conditions follow three patterns. A likely condition uses the present simple after if, and will in the main clause. An unlikely or imagined condition uses the simple past after if, and would in the main clause. An impossible condition in the past uses the past perfect after if, and would have with a past participle in the main clause.

slides.heading: Three kinds of clause
slides.body_md: A clause has its own **subject and verb**. A subordinate clause cannot stand alone and does the work of a noun, an adjective or an adverb.

rows: that, whether, if, what, why, how
We learnt *that the road was closed*
The road *that leads to the dam* was closed
an adverb: time, reason, condition, contrast, purpose
when, because, if, although, so that
We turned back *because the road was closed*

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of subordinate clause: noun clause, relative clause and adverb clause, with the work each does, how each begins and an example.

slides.narration: There are three kinds of subordinate clause. A noun clause does the work of a noun, as subject or object. A relative clause does the work of an adjective and describes a noun. An adverb clause does the work of an adverb and tells us the time, reason, condition, contrast or purpose. Ask what job the clause is doing.

slides.heading: Relative clauses: who, whom, whose, which, that
slides.body_md: Choose the pronoun by **who or what it replaces** and by its job in the clause.

rows: a lake whose water is clear
a bell which rings at noon
people or things, defining clauses only
the book that she lent me

visual.alt: Table of relative pronouns: who for people as subject, whom for people as object, whose for possession, which for things and that for defining clauses only.

slides.narration: In a relative clause, choose the pronoun by what it replaces. Who is for people as subject, whom for people as object, whose shows possession, which is for things, and that is for defining clauses only. Test by turning the clause into a short sentence and see which word it needs.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: defining or non-defining?
slides.body_md: *My brother has two kites. One kite, ______ (which / that) he made himself, is red.* Which word fits, and why?
bullets: **The clause** adds a detail about a kite we are already talking about.
**So it is non-defining:** it takes commas and cannot take *that*.
**Answer:** *which*.
**Test:** removing the clause leaves a complete, sensible sentence.

rows: adds extra detail about a noun already known

visual.alt: Table comparing defining and non-defining relative clauses by job, commas, use of that and effect of removing the clause.

slides.narration: Here the clause adds a detail about one kite we already know. That makes it non-defining. A non-defining clause takes commas and cannot use that, so the answer is which. A quick test: remove the clause. If the sentence still makes sense and says the same thing about which kite, the clause was non-defining.

slides.heading: Noun clauses
slides.body_md: A noun clause often follows a verb of **thinking, knowing, saying or asking**.

rows: I know that she is right
yes or no, or two choices
I wonder whether he has left

visual.alt: Table of noun clauses: that for statements, whether or if for yes-no questions or choices, and wh-words when the clause answers a question.

slides.narration: Noun clauses often follow verbs of thinking, knowing, saying or asking. Use that when the clause is a statement. Use whether or if for a yes or no question, or for two choices. Use a wh word, such as where, why or how, when the clause answers a question. In all of them, the clause keeps statement word order.

slides.heading: Check: which kind of clause?

rows: that, whether, if, what, why, how
We learnt *that the road was closed*
The road *that leads to the dam* was closed
an adverb: time, reason, condition, contrast, purpose
when, because, if, although, so that
We turned back *because the road was closed*

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of subordinate clause: noun clause, relative clause and adverb clause, with the work each does, how each begins and an example.

slides.narration: Your turn. Look at the sentence Mira knew that the shop had closed. What kind of clause are the words that the shop had closed? Ask what job the clause is doing.

slides.heading: Adverb clauses and their connectives
slides.body_md: Match the **connective to the idea**: a wrong connective changes the meaning.

rows: when, after, before, as soon as, until
We left as soon as the bell rang
She stayed in because it was raining
You will pass if you revise
Although it was late, we went on
He spoke slowly so that all could follow
It was so cold that the pond froze

visual.alt: Table of adverb clauses by idea: time, reason, condition, contrast, purpose and result, with connectives and an example for each.

slides.narration: Adverb clauses tell us time, reason, condition, contrast, purpose or result. Pick the connective for the idea. When, after and as soon as are for time. Because, since and as give a reason. If and unless give a condition. Although is for contrast. So that is for purpose. And never use although together with but in one sentence.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a gap with a clause and a tense
slides.body_md: *If the rain ______ (stop) soon, we ______ (play) on the lawn; if it stopped now, we ______ (play) with wet shoes.*
bullets: **Gap 1:** a likely condition: present simple, **stops**.
**Gap 2:** main clause for a likely condition: **will play**.
**Gap 3:** unlikely or imagined condition: **would play**.
**Check:** each *if* clause and its main clause belong to the same pattern.

rows: If it rains, we will stay in
If I had a bike, I would ride to school
If I had known, I would have called

visual.alt: Table of three kinds of condition: likely uses present simple and will, unlikely uses simple past and would, and impossible past uses past perfect and would have.

slides.narration: This example puts two patterns side by side. If the rain stops soon is a likely condition, so we use the present simple, and the main clause takes will. If it stopped now is imagined, so the simple past is used and the main clause takes would. Always match the if clause with its own main clause.

slides.heading: Check: choose the connective

rows: when, after, before, as soon as, until
We left as soon as the bell rang
She stayed in because it was raining
You will pass if you revise
Although it was late, we went on
He spoke slowly so that all could follow
It was so cold that the pond froze

visual.alt: Table of adverb clauses by idea: time, reason, condition, contrast, purpose and result, with connectives and an example for each.

slides.narration: Try this one. The lift was out of order, and so we climbed to the sixth floor. Which connective gives the right idea of reason?

slides.heading: Summary: tenses and clauses
bullets: Clue words choose the tense; read the whole paragraph first.
Earlier past event: past perfect; later: simple past.
Present perfect links to now; simple past is finished.
Conditions: present + will; past + would; past perfect + would have.
Clauses: noun (that, whether), relative (who, which), adverb (because, although).

nodes.label: Name the time and the order of events

visual.alt: Flow of the gap-filling routine: read the whole sentence, underline the clue words, name the time and the order of events, choose the form, then reread the paragraph.
visual.caption: SOYL five-move routine for a gap.

slides.narration: To sum up. Clue words choose the tense, so read the whole paragraph first. Use the past perfect for the earlier of two past events. The present perfect links to now. Match each if clause with its own main clause. And choose clauses by their job: noun clauses, relative clauses and adverb clauses, each with its own connectives.

slides.heading: Exam tips: gap filling
bullets: Read the whole passage before you fill the first gap.
Underline since, for, by the time, yesterday and other clues.
Reread the paragraph with your answers in place.
Check verbs, connectives and pronouns for each gap.
Common slips: a present form with a past clue; although together with but; that in a non-defining clause.

rows: By the time we came, the film started
By the time we came, the film had started
Although it was late but we left
Although it was late, we left
He asked where was I going
He asked where I was going

visual.alt: Table of five common grammar slips and their fixes: have gone with last Sunday, wrong sequence with by the time, although with but, question order in reported speech, and that in a non-defining clause.

slides.narration: Exam tips for gap filling. Read the whole passage before filling the first gap. Underline the clue words. After filling, reread the paragraph with your answers in place to catch any slip. Common slips are a present form with a past clue, although used together with but, and that used in a non-defining clause.

decks.title: Re-ordering and Transformation of Sentences — Part 2
goals: Change active sentences to passive, keeping tense and modals
Change direct speech to reported speech and back, shifting everything that must shift
Combine sentences with relative, noun and adverb clauses
Move between degrees and between simple, compound and complex sentences
Re-order jumbled word groups into one correct sentence

slides.heading: Re-ordering and Transformation
slides.body_md: In a transformation, the **meaning stays** and the **form changes**. This part teaches you which changes must be made together.

rows: object to subject; be in the right tense; past participle; by-phrase only if useful
tense, pronouns, time and place words, reporting verb, word order of questions
right connective or pronoun; commas for non-defining; tenses agree
meaning unchanged; no other / as ... as; although, not although ... but

visual.alt: Table of checklists for each transformation: active to passive, direct to reported speech, combining with clauses, and degrees and sentence types.

slides.narration: Welcome to part two. In a transformation task, the meaning of the sentence stays the same and only its form changes. The skill is knowing which changes must be made together. Each task type has its own checklist, and this part gives you those checklists, one after another.

slides.heading: Active to passive
slides.body_md: The passive **keeps the tense or modal** of the active and adds *be* in the matching form plus a past participle.

rows: Tea is made by the cook
The cook must have made tea

visual.alt: Table of active and passive forms across tenses and modals: the passive keeps the tense or modal of the active and adds be in the right form with the past participle.

slides.narration: In the passive, the object of the active sentence becomes the subject. The tense or modal stays the same, and you add the right form of be, followed by the past participle. The present continuous becomes is being made. The present perfect becomes has been made. A modal plus perfect becomes must have been made.

slides.heading: Five steps to the passive
slides.body_md: Add the **doer** with *by* only when it adds information.

nodes.label: Keep the tense; add be + past participle
Add by + doer only if needed

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for changing active to passive: find the object, make it the subject, keep the tense and add be with the past participle, add by and the doer only if needed, then check the meaning.
visual.caption: Five steps to the passive.

slides.narration: Here are five steps. Find the object. Make it the subject. Keep the tense and add be with the past participle. Add by and the doer only if the doer is needed, and leave it out when it is unknown or obvious. Finally check that the meaning is the same as in the active sentence.

slides.heading: Check: passive of a continuous tense

rows: Tea is made by the cook
The cook must have made tea

visual.alt: Table of active and passive forms across tenses and modals: the passive keeps the tense or modal of the active and adds be in the right form with the past participle.

slides.narration: Your turn. The cook is preparing the meal. Which sentence is the passive form? Remember that the tense must stay the present continuous.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a modal passive
slides.body_md: *The club can book the auditorium for the debate.* Change into the passive.
bullets: **Object:** *the auditorium*, which becomes the subject.
**Modal:** *can* stays; add *be* plus the past participle.
**Result:** *The auditorium can be booked by the club for the debate.*
**Check:** the modal and the meaning are unchanged.

nodes.label: Keep the tense; add be + past participle
Add by + doer only if needed

visual.alt: Flow of the steps for changing active to passive: find the object, make it the subject, keep the tense and add be with the past participle, add by and the doer only if needed, then check the meaning.
visual.caption: Five steps to the passive.

slides.narration: Here is a modal passive. The club can book the auditorium. The object, the auditorium, becomes the subject. The modal can stays, and we add be and the past participle: can be booked. So the passive is: The auditorium can be booked by the club for the debate. The modal and the meaning are both unchanged.

slides.heading: Reported speech: tense backshift
slides.body_md: After a **past reporting verb**, the reported verb steps one tense back.

visual.alt: Table of tense changes from direct to reported speech after a past reporting verb: present simple to simple past, present continuous to past continuous, present perfect and simple past to past perfect, will to would and can to could.

slides.narration: When the reporting verb is in the past, the reported verb steps one tense back. Present simple becomes simple past. Present continuous becomes past continuous. Present perfect and simple past both become past perfect. Will becomes would, and can becomes could. Universal truths and facts that are still true need not backshift.

slides.heading: Reported speech: pronouns, time and place
slides.body_md: Pronouns follow the **speaker and the listener**. Time and place words move away from the moment of speaking.

rows: the day before / the previous day
the next day / the following day

visual.alt: Table of word changes from direct to reported speech: now becomes then, today becomes that day, yesterday becomes the day before, tomorrow becomes the next day, here becomes there and ago becomes before.

slides.narration: Pronouns change to fit the speaker and the listener. Time and place words move away from the moment of speaking: now becomes then, yesterday becomes the day before, tomorrow becomes the next day, here becomes there. If the report is made on the same day, some time words can stay. Always ask when the report is made.

slides.heading: Check: report a statement

visual.alt: Table of tense changes from direct to reported speech after a past reporting verb: present simple to simple past, present continuous to past continuous, present perfect and simple past to past perfect, will to would and can to could.

slides.narration: Try one. Sheela said I am busy. Report the sentence later, using the past tense for the reporting verb. Remember to change both the tense and the pronoun.

slides.heading: Questions, commands and requests
slides.body_md: Reported questions use **statement word order** and no question mark.

rows: He said that he was late
She asked if I had come
He asked us not to shout

visual.alt: Table of reporting patterns: statements use said or told that, yes-no questions use asked if or whether with statement order, wh-questions keep the wh-word with statement order, and commands use a verb plus object plus to.

slides.narration: Each kind of sentence has its own reporting pattern. A statement uses said that or told that. A yes or no question uses asked if or whether, with statement word order. A wh question keeps its wh word, also with statement order. A command or request uses a verb like ordered or asked, with the object and to.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: report a short dialogue
slides.body_md: *Teacher: "Will you carry the charts, Imran?" Imran: "Yes, I will carry them after lunch."*
bullets: **Line 1:** a yes-no question: *The teacher asked Imran whether he would carry the charts.*
**Line 2:** a statement: *Imran replied that he would carry them after lunch.*
**Shifts:** *will* to *would*, *you* to *he*, *I* to *he*.
**Reporting verbs** are chosen to suit the line: *asked*, *replied*.

rows: He said that he was late
She asked if I had come
He asked us not to shout

visual.alt: Table of reporting patterns: statements use said or told that, yes-no questions use asked if or whether with statement order, wh-questions keep the wh-word with statement order, and commands use a verb plus object plus to.

slides.narration: Look at this short dialogue. The teacher asks Imran whether he will carry the charts. That is a yes or no question, so we use asked whether, statement order, and will becomes would. Imran replies that he would carry them after lunch. Choose reporting verbs to suit each line, such as asked and replied.

slides.heading: Combining sentences with clauses
slides.body_md: Decide first **how the two ideas are related**, then choose the clause.

rows: The lane, which is narrow, leads to the fort
She said that the lane was narrow
Because the lane was narrow, we walked

visual.alt: Table of ways to combine sentences: a relative clause for an extra fact about a noun, a noun clause with that for a statement as object, and an adverb clause for reason, time or contrast.

slides.narration: To combine sentences, first decide how the two ideas are related. An extra fact about a noun gives a relative clause. A statement that is the object of a verb gives a noun clause with that. A reason, a time or a contrast gives an adverb clause. Then choose the right connective and keep the tenses in step.

slides.heading: Check: combine with who

rows: The lane, which is narrow, leads to the fort
She said that the lane was narrow
Because the lane was narrow, we walked

visual.alt: Table of ways to combine sentences: a relative clause for an extra fact about a noun, a noun clause with that for a statement as object, and an adverb clause for reason, time or contrast.

slides.narration: Your turn. The tailor is a person, and he is the subject of had stitched. Which sentence joins the two sentences correctly? Choose the relative pronoun by what it replaces.

slides.heading: Degrees of comparison
slides.body_md: You can say the same thing in **three degrees**; the meaning must not change.

rows: No other hill is as high as this one
This hill is higher than any other hill
Few poets are as famous as she
She is more famous than most poets
She is one of the most famous poets

visual.alt: Table of three ways to say the same thing in positive, comparative and superlative degrees, for example no other hill is as high as this one, this hill is higher than any other, and this is the highest hill.

slides.narration: The same idea can be said in three degrees. The superlative says this is the highest hill. The comparative says this hill is higher than any other hill. The positive says no other hill is as high as this one. When you change degree, make sure the meaning does not change, and use than any other for the comparative.

slides.heading: Simple, compound and complex
slides.body_md: Count the **clauses and how they are joined**.

rows: Despite the rain, the match continued
two or more main clauses joined by and, but, so, or
It rained, but the match continued
one main clause + one or more subordinate clauses
Although it rained, the match continued

visual.alt: Table of three sentence types: simple has one main clause, compound joins main clauses with and, but, so or or, and complex has a main clause with a subordinate clause.

slides.narration: A simple sentence has one main clause. A compound sentence joins two or more main clauses with and, but, so or or. A complex sentence has a main clause with at least one subordinate clause. Changing between them means changing a phrase into a clause, or a clause into a coordinated main clause, without changing the meaning.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: re-order jumbled word groups
slides.body_md: *were thanked / The night watchmen / who had guarded the school / by the staff*
bullets: **Verb group:** *were thanked*; **subject:** *The night watchmen*.
**Relative clause:** straight after the noun it describes.
**Agent:** *by the staff* closes the passive.
**Result:** *The night watchmen who had guarded the school were thanked by the staff.*

nodes.label: Attach clauses next to the noun they describe
Place linking words and time phrases

visual.alt: Flow of re-ordering jumbled word groups: find the main verb group, find its subject, attach clauses next to the noun they describe, place linking words and time phrases, then read aloud and check.
visual.caption: SOYL five moves for a jumbled sentence.

slides.narration: Here is a jumbled sentence. Start with the verb group, were thanked, and its subject, the night watchmen. The relative clause, who had guarded the school, must come straight after the noun it describes. The agent, by the staff, closes the passive. Read it aloud to check that it sounds right.

slides.heading: Word order traps
slides.body_md: Some openers force **question order** in the main clause. Learn the few that matter.

rows: question order in the main clause
Not until dawn did the wind drop
Never had she seen such a crowd
Hardly had we sat down when the bell rang
question order in the main clause
Only after the repairs did the road reopen

visual.alt: Table of sentence openers that cause inversion: not until, never and seldom, hardly when, and only after, each followed by question order in the main clause.

slides.narration: Some sentence openers force question order in the main clause. Not until, never, seldom, hardly, and only after are the common ones. After them the helping verb comes before the subject. Spot the opener first, then place the remaining groups. These traps appear often in re-ordering tasks, so learn the list.

slides.heading: Summary: transformation and re-ordering
bullets: Passive: object to subject; keep tense or modal; be + past participle.
Reported speech: backshift, pronouns, time words, reporting verb, question order.
Combine: relative, noun or adverb clause by the relation of ideas.
Degrees and types: meaning unchanged.
Jumbled words: verb group, subject, clauses beside their nouns, openers.

rows: object to subject; be in the right tense; past participle; by-phrase only if useful
tense, pronouns, time and place words, reporting verb, word order of questions
right connective or pronoun; commas for non-defining; tenses agree
meaning unchanged; no other / as ... as; although, not although ... but

visual.alt: Table of checklists for each transformation: active to passive, direct to reported speech, combining with clauses, and degrees and sentence types.

slides.narration: To sum up. In the passive, keep the tense and add be with the past participle. In reported speech, change tense, pronouns, time words and the reporting verb together. Combine sentences by the relation between ideas. Change degrees and sentence types without changing meaning. For jumbled words, find the verb group and the subject, and keep clauses beside their nouns.

slides.heading: Exam tips: transformation
bullets: Make all the changes a task needs; one missed shift loses the mark.
Keep the meaning: do not add or drop information.
Check commas and question marks after each change.
Read your jumbled sentence aloud before you write it.
Common slips: backshift forgotten; question order kept in a reported question; although together with but.

rows: By the time we came, the film started
By the time we came, the film had started
Although it was late but we left
Although it was late, we left
He asked where was I going
He asked where I was going

visual.alt: Table of five common grammar slips and their fixes: have gone with last Sunday, wrong sequence with by the time, although with but, question order in reported speech, and that in a non-defining clause.

slides.narration: Exam tips for transformation. Make every change that a task needs, because one missed shift can lose the mark. Keep the meaning the same. Check commas and question marks after each change. Read a re-ordered sentence aloud. Common slips are forgetting the backshift, keeping question order in a reported question, and using although together with but.

notes.title: Grammar — Class 11 notes

sections.heading: 1. The grammar section at a glance
sections.body_md:
Class 11 has no board exam: the school annual examination carries **7 marks** for grammar. Tasks are **gap filling with tenses and clauses** and **re-ordering and transformation** of sentences.

SOYL chapter tests use the class-default pattern: objective questions on forms, 2- and 3-mark transformations, 5-mark paragraph tasks and 4-mark gap or error passages.

key_terms.definition_md: Choosing or writing the right word or form for a blank in a sentence or paragraph.

sections.heading: 2. Tenses and time clues
sections.body_md:
Every tense is a time (present, past, future) plus a form (simple, continuous, perfect, perfect continuous).

**Clues:** *every day* → present simple; *now* → present continuous; *since, for, so far, yet* → present perfect (continuous); *yesterday, ago, last year* → simple past; *by the time* with an earlier past event → past perfect; *by tomorrow* → future perfect.

Use the **present perfect** when the result or experience matters now and the **simple past** for a finished event.

key_terms.definition_md: A form that looks back from a point in time: has/had/will have + past participle.
A form that shows an action in progress: be + -ing.

sections.heading: 3. Tense sequence, conditions and consistency
sections.body_md:
Two past events: the earlier takes the past perfect, the later the simple past. A time clause about the future takes a present form (*when I reach home*).

**Conditions:** likely = *if* + present, *will*; unlikely = *if* + past, *would*; impossible past = *if* + past perfect, *would have* + past participle. A *wish* about the past takes the past perfect.

Tense is not the same as time: a timetable may use the present simple for the future. Read the whole sentence for clues.

sections.heading: 4. Clauses: noun, relative and adverb
sections.body_md:
A **noun clause** does the work of a noun (*that, whether, if, what, why, how*). A **relative clause** describes a noun (*who* for people as subject, *whom* as object, *whose* for possession, *which* for things, *that* in defining clauses only). A **non-defining** clause adds extra detail and takes commas; a **defining** clause picks out which one and takes none.

An **adverb clause** gives time (*when, after*), reason (*because, since*), condition (*if, unless*), contrast (*although*), purpose (*so that*) or result (*so ... that*). Do not use *although* and *but* together.

sections.heading: 5. Active and passive
sections.body_md:
In the passive, the object of the active sentence becomes the subject, the tense or modal is kept, and **be** in the right form plus the **past participle** is added: *is made, is being made, has been made, was made, will be made, can be made, must have been made*.

Use *by* and the doer only when it adds information. The passive is chosen when the doer is unknown or unimportant.

With verbs of saying, two passives are possible: *It is said that ...* and *The subject is said to ...*.

sections.heading: 6. Reported speech
sections.body_md:
After a past reporting verb the reported verb backshifts: present simple → simple past, present continuous → past continuous, present perfect and simple past → past perfect, *will* → *would*, *can* → *could*.

Pronouns follow the speaker and listener. Time and place words move away: *now* → *then*, *yesterday* → *the day before*, *tomorrow* → *the next day*, *here* → *there*, *ago* → *before*. On the same day some can stay. Facts still true need no backshift.

Questions are reported with *if/whether* or the *wh-word* in statement order; commands and requests with a verb plus object plus *(not) to*.

sections.heading: 7. Combining, degrees, sentence types and re-ordering
sections.body_md:
**Combining:** relate the ideas, then choose a relative clause (extra fact about a noun), a noun clause with *that* (a statement as object) or an adverb clause (reason, time, contrast).

**Degrees:** *the highest hill* = *higher than any other hill* = *no other hill is as high as this one*. **Types:** simple (one main clause), compound (main clauses joined by *and, but, so, or*), complex (main clause plus subordinate clause).

**Re-ordering:** find the verb group and its subject; keep a clause beside the noun it describes; place openers such as *not until* with question order; read aloud.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Marks (school paper):** grammar 7 = gap filling with tenses and clauses; re-ordering and transformation. SOYL chapter tests use objective questions, 2- and 3-mark transformations, 5-mark paragraph tasks and 4-mark gap or error passages.

**How marks are awarded**
- Objective and gap items: the one correct form; every correct alternative is accepted.
- Transformation: one mark for each change that the task needs (for example tense, pronoun, time word) with the meaning kept.
- Paragraph tasks: one mark for each error corrected or each pair joined; consistent tenses and clear punctuation.

**Common mistakes**
1. A present form with a past clue; the present perfect with *yesterday* or *last week*.
2. Missing the earlier event: the past perfect forgotten.
3. *Although* together with *but*; *that* in a non-defining clause.
4. Question order kept in a reported question.
5. A time word or pronoun left unchanged in reported speech made later.
6. A modal or *been* dropped in the passive.
7. A jumbled sentence not read aloud.

**Time:** read the whole paragraph or sentence before you fill the first gap or make the first change.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** knew. The main clause has *would* plus a base verb, the pattern of an unlikely present condition, so the *if* clause takes the simple past.

questions.stem_md: I wish I ______ the date of the exam earlier; now I have too little time to prepare.
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** had known. The regret is about the past, since the shortage of time is the result now. A wish about a past event takes the past perfect.

questions.stem_md: In which sentence do the words in italics form a noun clause?

options.text_md: The bus *that was late* was empty.
The teacher knows *why the bus was late*.
The driver, *who was new*, lost the way.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The teacher knows *why the bus was late*. *Why the bus was late* is what the teacher knows: the object of the verb. The other clauses are an adjective clause, an adverb clause of time and a non-defining adjective clause.

questions.stem_md: Which sentence means that every student in the class got a scholarship?

options.text_md: The students who studied hard got scholarships.
The students, who studied hard, got scholarships.
Only the students who studied hard got scholarships.
The students who got scholarships studied hard.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The students, who studied hard, got scholarships. Commas make the clause non-defining: it adds a comment on all the students. Without commas, the clause picks out some students from a larger group.

questions.stem_md: Which sentence is the passive form of: *The jury should have announced the result earlier.*?

options.text_md: The result should have been announced earlier by the jury.
The result should be announced earlier by the jury.
The result should have announced earlier by the jury.
The result was to be announced earlier by the jury.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The result should have been announced earlier by the jury. Both the modal and the perfect must carry over: *should have* plus *been* plus the past participle. Dropping *been* breaks the passive; dropping *have* changes the time.

questions.stem_md: Ira said, "I will submit my file tomorrow." Which is the correct report, made a week later?

options.text_md: Ira said that she will submit her file tomorrow.
Ira said that she would submit her file the next day.
Ira said that I would submit my file the next day.
Ira said that she would submit her file tomorrow.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Ira said that she would submit her file the next day. Three things change together: the verb backshifts, the pronouns follow the speaker, and the time word shifts because the report is made much later.

questions.stem_md: The teacher asked Dev, "Have you finished the exercise?" Choose the correct report.

options.text_md: The teacher asked Dev had he finished the exercise.
The teacher asked Dev that he had finished the exercise.
The teacher asked Dev if he has finished the exercise.
The teacher asked Dev if he had finished the exercise.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The teacher asked Dev if he had finished the exercise. A yes/no question is reported with *if* or *whether*, in statement word order, with the tense backshifted and the pronoun changed.

questions.stem_md: The officer said to the guard, "Do not open the gate before noon." Which is the correct report?

options.text_md: The officer ordered the guard not to open the gate before noon.
The officer ordered the guard that he did not open the gate before noon.
The officer ordered the guard do not open the gate before noon.
The officer ordered the guard to be not opened the gate before noon.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The officer ordered the guard not to open the gate before noon. A command is reported with a verb such as *ordered*, the object, then *not to* plus the base verb.

questions.stem_md: Which sentence has the same meaning as: *The Nilgiri line is the most scenic route in the region.*?

options.text_md: The Nilgiri line is as scenic as any other route in the region.
No other route in the region is more scenic as the Nilgiri line.
No other route in the region is as scenic as the Nilgiri line.
The Nilgiri line is scenic than other routes in the region.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** No other route in the region is as scenic as the Nilgiri line. A superlative can become the negative positive degree: *no other ... as ... as*.

questions.stem_md: Which complex sentence matches the compound sentence *He is wealthy, but he is not happy.*?

options.text_md: Because he is wealthy, he is not happy.
Unless he is wealthy, he is not happy.
Although he is wealthy, he is not happy.
Until he is wealthy, he is not happy.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Although he is wealthy, he is not happy. *But* shows contrast, and *although* introduces a clause of contrast. The other connectives change the meaning.

questions.stem_md: The sentence *Sneha told Pooja that she had won the prize* could mean that either girl won. Which rewrite makes it clear that Pooja won?

options.text_md: Sneha told Pooja that Pooja had won the prize.
Sneha told Pooja that she herself had won the prize.
Sneha told her friend that she had won the prize.
Sneha told Pooja that the prize had been won by her.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Sneha told Pooja that Pooja had won the prize. The problem is a pronoun that can point two ways. Repeating the name removes the doubt; the other versions still leave a pronoun open or point to Sneha.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In *I will call you when I reach Pune*, the verb after *when* is in the present tense although the call is in the future.

**Reason (R):** In adverb clauses of time, English uses a present form to refer to future time.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The assertion describes the pattern and the reason states the rule behind it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The sentence *The village whose well had dried up received a water tanker* is correct.

**Reason (R):** *Whose* is used only for people and never for things.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The sentence is correct, and *whose* is also used for things and places, so the reason is false.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** *Although she was tired, but she finished the report* is a correct complex sentence.

**Reason (R):** *Although* already introduces the clause of contrast, so *but* is not needed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Using both words repeats the contrast, so the assertion is false while the reason is true.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a passive sentence, the object of the active sentence becomes the subject.

**Reason (R):** The passive is chosen when the doer of the action is unknown or unimportant.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true. The first describes how the passive is built, and the second states when it is chosen: neither explains the other.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A reporter may say *He said that the Earth moves round the Sun* without any backshift.

**Reason (R):** Backshift is not required when the reported statement is still true at the time of reporting.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The reporter leaves the verb unchanged because the fact has not stopped being true; the reason explains why.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A reporter on the same day may keep *now* unchanged in *She said that she was busy now*.

**Reason (R):** *Now* always changes to *then* in reported speech.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The time word changes only when the report is made at a different time; on the same day it can stay. The reason says *always*, which is false.

questions.stem_md: In *I know that she is honest*, the words *that she is honest* form a noun clause.
questions.solution_md: **True.** The clause is the object of *know*: it answers *know what?*

questions.stem_md: *He asked me where was I going* is correct reported speech.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A reported question uses statement word order and no question mark: *where I was going*.

questions.stem_md: *That* can introduce a non-defining relative clause, as in *My cousin, that lives in Surat, called today*.
questions.solution_md: **False.** A non-defining clause takes *who* or *which*. *That* is kept for defining clauses.

questions.stem_md: Ananya ___ (work) on the model since morning, but she ___ (not finish) it yet.
questions.solution_md: *Since morning* and *yet* both link the past to now: **has been working** and **has not finished** (*has worked* and *hasn't finished* are also accepted).

questions.stem_md: By the time the chief guest ___ (arrive), the students ___ (rehearse) the song for an hour, and the hall ___ (already, fill) with parents.
questions.solution_md: The arrival is the past reference point: **arrived**. Rehearsing ran up to it: **had been rehearsing** (*had rehearsed* is also accepted). The hall filled before it: **had already filled** (*was already filling* is also accepted).

questions.stem_md: The author ___ (possession) novel won the prize will speak ___ (time) the book fair opens, and we hope ___ (noun clause) the hall will be full.
questions.solution_md: The novel belongs to the author: **whose**. The talk is timed by the fair opening: **when** (*once*, *after* and *as soon as* are also accepted). A full statement after *hope* needs **that**.

questions.stem_md: If I ___ (be) you, I ___ (apologise) to the coach now.
questions.solution_md: An unlikely present condition takes the simple past in the *if* clause: **were** (*was* is also accepted) and *would* plus the base verb: **would apologise**.

questions.stem_md: The old bridge ___ (repair) at the moment, so vehicles ___ (divert) through the market road since last week.
questions.solution_md: *At the moment* needs the present continuous passive: **is being repaired**. *Since last week* needs the present perfect passive: **have been diverted**.

questions.stem_md: The guide said, "We will leave tomorrow." Reported a week later: The guide said that they ___ leave ___ .
questions.solution_md: *Will* backshifts to **would**, and *tomorrow* becomes **the next day** (*the following day* and *the day after* are also accepted) because the report is made later.

questions.stem_md: Match each connective with the idea it expresses in an adverb clause.
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). These are the four connective families the notes list for adverb clauses.

questions.stem_md: Match each word in direct speech with its usual form in reported speech (reported at a later time).
questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each word moves one step away from the speaker's moment.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the word groups to make a sentence about volunteers and the principal, with the relative clause in its right place.
questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (b) → (c) → (a). The relative clause must sit straight after the noun it describes, and the passive verb group comes before the agent.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the word groups to make a sentence about a power cut, using the inversion that follows the opening group.

options.text_md: Not until the lights went out

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (d) → (c) → (b) → (a). After *not until* the clause is followed by the question order *did we realise*; the noun clause comes last.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Arrange the word groups to make a sentence about a bus and a flooded road. The sentence begins with the group that starts with a capital letter.

options.text_md: which was carrying the cricket team

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (c) → (d) → (b) → (a) → (e). The opening clause is followed by its main clause. The relative clause stays beside *the bus*, and *on time* closes the sentence.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: Rewrite in the passive voice: *The committee should have informed the parents about the change earlier.*
questions.solution_md: The object becomes the subject; *should have* stays; *been* plus the past participle completes the passive.

answer.model_answer_md: The parents should have been informed about the change earlier (by the committee). The modal and the perfect are both kept, and the past participle follows *been*.

marking_scheme.step: Object becomes subject with *should have been informed*
Rest of the sentence correct and meaning unchanged

questions.stem_md: Report in indirect speech, a week later: *Meghna said to Ila, "I will send you the photographs the day after tomorrow."*
questions.solution_md: Reporting verb *told* with the listener; *will* to *would*; *I/you* to *she/her*; *the day after tomorrow* to *two days later*.

answer.model_answer_md: Meghna told Ila that she would send her the photographs two days later. Will becomes would, the pronouns change, and the time word shifts.

marking_scheme.step: Time expression changed and the sentence reads smoothly

questions.stem_md: Join with a relative clause using *whose*: *I bought a bag. Its zip was broken.*
questions.solution_md: *Whose* replaces the possessive *its* and links the clause to *bag*.

answer.model_answer_md: I bought a bag whose zip was broken. The word whose replaces its and joins the second sentence to the noun bag.

questions.stem_md: Change into a complex sentence: *In spite of his injury, Dhruv completed the race.*
questions.solution_md: A phrase of contrast becomes an *although* clause with a subject and a verb in the past.

answer.model_answer_md: Although he was injured, Dhruv completed the race. The phrase of contrast has become a clause with its own subject and verb.

marking_scheme.step: Subordinate clause with *although* (or *though*) and a verb

questions.stem_md: Explain the difference in meaning between: (a) *Nisha has lost her keys.* (b) *Nisha lost her keys.*
questions.solution_md: The present perfect connects the loss to the present result; the simple past reports a finished event with no link to now.

answer.model_answer_md: Sentence (a) tells us the keys are still missing now, so the past event matters at present. Sentence (b) only reports a past event; it does not say whether the keys were found afterwards.

marking_scheme.step: (b): finished past event, no link stated

questions.stem_md: Explain how the meaning changes if commas are removed from: *The shirts, which were stitched in Surat, were sold out.*
questions.solution_md: Commas make the clause non-defining (extra detail about all); without them it is defining (selects some).

answer.model_answer_md: With commas, all the shirts were stitched in Surat and the clause only adds a detail. Without commas, the clause picks out only those shirts that were stitched in Surat from a larger set.

marking_scheme.step: With commas: extra detail about all the shirts
Without commas: selects some shirts out of a larger group

questions.stem_md: Complete the sentence with a suitable adverb clause of reason: *Rohit stayed behind after practice ______.*
questions.solution_md: Any clause that starts with *because*, *as* or *since* and gives a sensible reason in the past tense earns both marks.

answer.model_answer_md: Rohit stayed behind after practice because he wanted to perfect his serve. The clause begins with because and keeps the past tense.

marking_scheme.step: Clause begins with a connective of reason
Sensible reason; tense consistent with the main clause

questions.stem_md: Rewrite as a compound sentence: *Having missed the first bus, Anil walked to school.*
questions.solution_md: Two main clauses joined by *so* (or *and*, *therefore*); no clause depends on the other.

answer.model_answer_md: Anil missed the first bus, so he walked to school. The participle phrase becomes a clause joined by the coordinating word so.

marking_scheme.step: Two main clauses with a coordinating link

questions.stem_md: Change into direct speech: *Tara told the receptionist that she had left her umbrella at the hotel the day before and asked her to check.*
questions.solution_md: Reverse the changes: past perfect to simple past, *she/her* to *I/my*, *the day before* to *yesterday*, and the request into a polite question.

answer.model_answer_md: Tara said to the receptionist, "I left my umbrella at the hotel yesterday. Could you please check?" The tense moves forward, the pronouns change and the day before becomes yesterday.

marking_scheme.step: Statement part: tense, pronoun and time word reversed
Request written as a direct request with quotation marks

questions.stem_md:
Rewrite each sentence as directed.

(i) *The old caretaker was loved by all the children.* (active voice)

(ii) *"Where are you going?" she asked me.* (reported speech)

(iii) *Pallavi is taller than any other girl in the class.* (superlative degree)
questions.solution_md: One rule per part: agent to subject; reported question with statement order and backshift; comparative to superlative.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) All the children loved the old caretaker. (ii) She asked me where I was going. (iii) Pallavi is the tallest girl in the class. Each answer follows one rule: the agent becomes the subject, the question takes statement order with a backshift, and the comparison becomes a superlative.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) reported question with statement order and backshift

questions.stem_md:
Report the exchange in two or three sentences.

Jai: "Did you watch the final?"

Ravi: "No, I was travelling. I will watch the recording tonight."
questions.solution_md: Question: *asked whether* with *had watched*. Reply: *had not*, *had been travelling*. Addition: *would watch*, *tonight* to *that night*.

answer.model_answer_md: Jai asked Ravi whether he had watched the final. Ravi replied that he had not, because he had been travelling, and added that he would watch the recording that night. The question takes statement order, and every tense and time word shifts with the report.

marking_scheme.step: Question reported with whether/if and backshift
Reply reported with correct tense and pronouns
Second statement with would and the time word changed

questions.stem_md: Rewrite the paragraph, correcting every tense error: *Yesterday Hari goes to the post office. He waited in the queue for an hour before the clerk call his name. Then he found that he has forgotten the form.*
questions.solution_md: The whole account is in the past. *goes* becomes *went*, *call* becomes *called*, *has forgotten* becomes *had forgotten* (the earlier event).

answer.model_answer_md: Yesterday Hari went to the post office. He waited in the queue for an hour before the clerk called his name. Then he found that he had forgotten the form. The errors were goes, call and has forgotten: the passage is in the past, and the forgetting came before the finding.

marking_scheme.step: has forgotten corrected to had forgotten

questions.stem_md:
Combine the four sentences into one complex sentence containing one relative clause and one adverb clause. Do not use *but*.

*The bridge connected the two villages. It was built in 1962. It collapsed in the flood. The flood was unusually heavy.*
questions.solution_md: Join the first facts with a relative clause (*which ... built in 1962*) and the cause with an adverb clause (*because/as ... heavy*), keeping the past tense.

answer.model_answer_md: The bridge, which connected the two villages and was built in 1962, collapsed in the flood because the flood was unusually heavy. One acceptable version uses a which clause for the first facts and a because clause for the cause; another may begin with As the flood was unusually heavy.

marking_scheme.step: A correct adverb clause of reason
One complete sentence, tenses consistent, no but

questions.stem_md: A student writes: *If I will get the scholarship, I would join the college in Pune.* (i) Name the error. (ii) Write a corrected sentence for a likely condition. (iii) Write one for an unlikely condition.
questions.solution_md: The two clauses belong to different patterns. Likely = present simple + *will*; unlikely = past simple + *would*.

answer.model_answer_md: The error is mixing patterns: will after if, with would in the main clause. Likely: If I get the scholarship, I will join the college in Pune. Unlikely: If I got the scholarship, I would join the college in Pune. Each pair keeps if and the main clause in step.

questions.stem_md: Two classmates change *People say that the old fort is haunted* into the passive. Rani writes *It is said that the old fort is haunted.* Sam writes *The old fort is said haunted.* Whose sentence is correct? Say what is wrong with the other and give a second correct version.
questions.solution_md: Impersonal passive: *It is said that ...* or *Subject is said to ...* with the infinitive.

answer.model_answer_md: Rani is correct. Sam leaves out to be, so the sentence is incomplete after said. A second correct version is: The old fort is said to be haunted. Both correct forms start from the same active sentence, one with a dummy it and one with the subject moved forward.

questions.stem_md:
Rewrite the paragraph, correcting all the tense errors (about 80 to 120 words).

*Last summer our class visits a village near Pune. By the time we reached the school, the children are already waiting for us with garlands. They have been singing since the morning, and their teacher tells us that they practise for two weeks. We sit under a tree while the villagers serve lunch. When we leave, everyone waves until the bus has disappeared from sight.*
questions.solution_md: The errors are *visits* to *visited*, *are* to *were*, *have been singing* to *had been singing*, *tells* to *told*, *practise* to *had practised*, *sit* to *sat* / *serve* to *served* / *leave* to *left* / *has disappeared* to *had disappeared* as the account moves back into the past.

answer.model_answer_md: Last summer our class visited a village near Pune. By the time we reached the school, the children were already waiting for us with garlands. They had been singing since the morning, and their teacher told us that they had practised for two weeks. We sat under a tree while the villagers served lunch. When we left, everyone waved until the bus had disappeared from sight. The whole account keeps to the past; earlier events use the past perfect, and the singing that was still going on uses the past perfect continuous.

marking_scheme.step: Opening verbs in the simple past (visited, were waiting)
Earlier action in the past perfect (had been singing)
Remaining verbs in the past (sat, served, left)
Last clause: had disappeared; paragraph consistent throughout

questions.stem_md:
Report this conversation in a paragraph of about 80 to 120 words.

Nalini: "Have you chosen a topic for the science fair?"

Joel: "Not yet. I am thinking about a water filter."

Nalini: "Please do not choose that. Three groups made filters last year."

Joel: "Thanks for telling me. I will look for something new."
questions.solution_md: Question: *asked whether he had chosen*. Statement: *replied that he had not yet ... was thinking*. Request: *requested him not to choose*; *made* to *had made*, *last year* to *the year before*. Thanks and promise: *thanked her ... would look*.

answer.model_answer_md: Nalini asked Joel whether he had chosen a topic for the science fair. Joel replied that he had not yet and that he was thinking about a water filter. Nalini requested him not to choose that, explaining that three groups had made filters the year before. Joel thanked her for telling him and said that he would look for something new. Each line changes by its type: a question, a statement, a request and a plain statement, with tenses, pronouns and time words shifted together.

marking_scheme.step: Question: asked whether, statement order, had chosen
Request reported with not to; reason in the past perfect with the time word changed
Reporting verbs varied and the paragraph reads smoothly

questions.stem_md:
Rewrite each sentence of this notice in the passive voice (about 80 to 120 words in all).

*The school will hold the annual quiz next Friday. The Class 11 teams have already prepared the questions. The principal is going to present the trophy. Students should not bring mobile phones. The librarian must lock the library before the event.*
questions.solution_md: Each sentence needs the right form: *will be held*, *have been prepared*, *is going to be presented*, *should not be brought*, *must be locked*.

answer.model_answer_md: The annual quiz will be held by the school next Friday. The questions have already been prepared by the Class 11 teams. The trophy is going to be presented by the principal. Mobile phones should not be brought by students. The library must be locked by the librarian before the event. In each sentence the object has become the subject, and the helping verbs of the tense or modal are kept before been or be.

marking_scheme.step: must be locked; meaning kept throughout

questions.stem_md:
Join each pair of marked sentences using the clause named, and write the whole paragraph (about 80 to 120 words).

*(1) Kavya trained every morning. She wanted to win the district race. (reason)* *(2) The coach was impressed. He had watched her closely. (relative clause)* *(3) The race began. It rained heavily. (time clause)* *(4) She won by two seconds. Everyone knew this. (noun clause)*
questions.solution_md: (1) adverb clause of reason with *because*. (2) relative clause with *who*, set off by commas because the coach is already known. (3) adverb clause of time with *when/as*. (4) noun clause with *that* as object of *knew*.

answer.model_answer_md: Kavya trained every morning because she wanted to win the district race. The coach, who had watched her closely, was impressed. When the race began, it rained heavily, yet she ran steadily. Everyone knew that she had won by two seconds. The clause words are because, who, when and that: each links the second idea to the first, and the tenses stay in the past throughout.

marking_scheme.step: Complete paragraph with consistent tenses and clear punctuation

questions.stem_md:
This paragraph has five errors of different kinds. Rewrite it correctly and name the kind of error you fix in each sentence (about 80 to 120 words).

*(1) Although the match was close, but our team played with confidence. (2) The captain, that had injured her ankle, still led from the front. (3) By the time the final over began, we scored forty runs. (4) The crowd was asked by the umpire stay behind the rope. (5) After the match, the coach told us that we play well.*
questions.solution_md: The five errors are a doubled connective, a wrong relative pronoun, a tense sequence slip, a missing *to* in a passive with an infinitive, and a missing backshift in reported speech.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Although the match was close, our team played with confidence: but removed, because although already marks the contrast. (2) The captain, who had injured her ankle, still led from the front: that is not used in a non-defining clause. (3) By the time the final over began, we had scored forty runs: earlier action in the past perfect. (4) The crowd was asked by the umpire to stay behind the rope: to is needed after asked. (5) After the match, the coach told us that we had played well: backshift after told.

questions.stem_md: A friend says: "Tenses are only about time: past, present and future." In about 80 to 120 words, say how far you agree, using at least three sentences of your own as evidence.
questions.solution_md: A good answer gives a judgement and at least three examples where the form and the time differ: present for future schedule, perfect for present relevance, past form for unreal present.

answer.model_answer_md: I agree only in part. Tenses do show time: She left yesterday is clearly past. But the link between tense and time is not exact. The train leaves at six tomorrow uses the present simple for a future event, because it follows a timetable. Nisha has lost her keys uses a past action to say something about now. And If I knew, I would tell you uses a past form for a situation that is unlikely at present. So tense also shows plans, results and possibility, and the clues in the sentence must be read as well.

marking_scheme.step: A clear judgement (partly agree, with reasons)
First valid example of tense and time not matching
Conclusion that reads the whole sentence for clues; clear expression
